'''William A. Edelstein''' {{small|[[Institute of Physics|FInstP]]}} (November 21, 1944 – February 10, 2014) was an American physicist. One of the key developers of [[magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI), he was part of the team that developed the first full-body MRI scanner at the [[University of Aberdeen]], [[Scotland]], and was the primary inventor of spin-warp imaging, which is still used in all commercial MRI systems.<ref name="obituary">{{cite news|author=Frederick N. Rasmussen |title=Dr. William A. Edelstein, MRI pioneer|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2014/02/21/dr-william-a-edelstein-mri-pioneer/|access-date=4 April 2015|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=February 21, 2015}}</ref>

Edelstein's contributions to MRI technology include pulse sequence optimization, radio-frequency-coil and gradient-coil design, circuitry improvements, high field imaging, acoustic noise reduction, and the NMR Phased Array.<ref name="illinois">{{cite news|last1=Schwink|first1=Siv|title=Physics Illinois alumnus recognized for lifetime of pioneering contributions to MRI|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/news/34406|access-date=1 January 2025|work=[[University of Illinois]]|date=May 15, 2013}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Edelstein was born in [[Gloversville, New York]], to Arthur S. Edelstein, an optometrist, and Hannah Edelstein. His father was stationed in [[Burma|Myanmar]] with the [[United States Air Force]] and did not meet his son until he was a year old.<ref name="jean">{{cite web|last1=Edelstein|first1=Jean Hannah|title=William A. Edelstein, 1944 – 2014|url=http://www.jeanhannahedelstein.com/william-a-edelstein-1944-2014/#more-1087|access-date=4 April 2015}}</ref> His family was Jewish.<ref>{{cite news|title=Obituary: Arthur S. Edelstein|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/chicagotribune/obituary.aspx?pid=141485833|access-date=4 April 2015|work=[[Chicago Tribune]]|date=April 4, 2010}}</ref>

He grew up in [[Schenectady, New York]] and [[Utica, New York]] before moving to [[Northbrook, Illinois]], where he graduated from [[Glenbrook North High School]] in 1962. He received a Bachelor of Science in physics from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] in 1965, graduating summa cum laude. He then attended [[Harvard University]], earning a master's degree in physics in 1967, followed by his Ph.D. in 1974. His thesis, on nuclear physics, was supervised by [[Robert Pound]].<ref name="obituary"/>

Academic awards include the Edmund James Scholar and the 1965 Brahana Prize in Mathematics at the University of Illinois, where he was a member of [[Phi Beta Kappa]].

==Career==
Edelstein moved to Scotland, where he had two three-year postdoctoral research fellowships: the first at the [[University of Glasgow]], where he worked on gravitational wave detection from 1974 to 1977, and the second at the [[University of Aberdeen]] from 1977 to 1980, where he was part of the group that performed the first full-body human MRI scan.

Edelstein worked for the [[General Electric]] Research and Development Centre in Schenectady from 1980 to 2001, where he continued to work in a group which included colleague Paul Bottomley on the development of GE's MRI technology. He was named a Coolidge Fellow, the highest corporate scientific honor bestowed by GE R&D, and won the GE Dushman Award for “Outstanding Technical Work on Nuclear Magnetic Resonance, Imaging and Spectroscopy."<ref name="cv">{{cite web|last1=Edelstein|first1=William A.|title=William A. Edelstein curriculum vitae|url=http://www.mri.jhu.edu/~edelstei/edelstein.cv|publisher=Johns Hopkins University|access-date=4 April 2015}}</ref>

After 21 years at GE, he founded MRScience LLC, through which he continued to work on the technology.<ref name="obituary"/> He also served as a visiting scientist at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] in New York and a senior research associate at [[Case Western Reserve University]] in Ohio.<ref name="illinois"/> Edelstein became a Visiting Distinguished Professor of Radiology at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 2007.

During his career, he held 49 patents.<ref name="illinois"/>

==Recognition==
He was named a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1988, [[Institute of Physics]] in 1996 and [[International Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine]] (ISMRM) in 1997.<ref name="cv"/>

He won the Gold Medal from the ISMRM in 1990, and the AIP Prize for Industrial Applications of Physics from the [[American Institute of Physics]] in 2005.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ismrm.org/Memoriam/edelstein.htm|title = In Memoriam}}</ref> He received an honorary doctorate from the University of Aberdeen in 2007<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abdn.ac.uk/mediareleases/release.php?id=986|title=Sir Steve Redgrave honoured by Aberdeen|work=[[University of Aberdeen]]|date=26 June 2007}}</ref> and the 2013 Alumni Achievement Award from the [[University of Illinois]].<ref name="illinois"/>

==''Star Trek'' controversy==
In 2010, Edelstein presented a paper at a meeting of the [[American Physical Society]] in which he disclosed his findings that the reason that space travel at the speed of light had not been achieved is that according to [[Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity]], spaceships would be exposed at such speeds to a dose of radiation that would be fatal to crew members. Edelstein suggested that his calculations showed the crew of the ''[[Starship Enterprise]]'' would have suffered this fate if their travels had not been fiction. ''[[Star Trek]]'' fans protested volubly on numerous internet discussion boards.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn18532-starship-pilots-speed-kills-especially-warp-speed.html|title=Starship pilots: speed kills, especially warp speed |date=17 February 2010 |first= Valerie |last=Jamieson |access-date=4 April 2015}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Edelstein met his wife, psychologist Fiona (''née'' Jones), while living in Glasgow. They married in 1977 and had a son, physicist Arthur Edelstein, and two daughters, writer <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jeanhannahedelstein|title = Jean Hannah Edelstein &#124; the Guardian|website = [[TheGuardian.com]]}}</ref> Jean Hannah Edelstein and linguist Elspeth (Edelstein) Barras.<ref>https://www.abdn.ac.uk/people/elspeth.edelstein/. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240412182304/https://www.abdn.ac.uk/people/elspeth.edelstein/ |date=2020-08-12 }}</ref>

Edelstein died of lung cancer on February 10, 2014, at his home in [[Northwood, Baltimore]].<ref name="obituary"/>
